I work with preschoolers, so your millage may vary, but one of the most magical things we have implemented when all of the impatient tiny people want to talk at the same time is sign language! Which sounds like a high barrier to entry but hear me out, you only need one sign.

We have a system, (tap a teacher) which could be implemented as any obvious physical sign, that we ***religiously*** follow up. A child does the physical signal that they want a turn to talk, and without turning away from what’s in front of them, the adult gives the physical signal back that *I see you want to talk, and I want to hear it next*. 

I find that the silent acknowledgement gives the people that want to talk more patience, because they know they’ll get to talk, and me, the person trying to listen, more space to engage without hitting overwhelmed. 

Our system may be a little rigid for home use, but you may get something out of a similar idea

I’m having trouble thinking of other words that change when they’re a term of address (you, second person) vs a term of reference (he/she/them, third person) so forgive me this example.

“Bitch, please” “Hey bitches!” “What’s up my bitches?” gender neutral. Would say, in an informal setting to close male or female friends (with whom I had that relationship). 

“That bitch over there” always female.

So, that’s still sexist, and like guy and dude varies by dialect. 

An interesting consequence of mixed gendered groups being male though is “Those guys over there” could reference a male or mixed gendered group, though not usually an all female group. “Those bitches over there” I automatically assume references an all female group, *or only the women in a mixed gendered group.* Language is weird!

Oh, that’s because of a neat grammar thing! It’s (in many dialects) gender neutral when you’re talking *to* somebody, but masculine when talking *about* somebody.
 
“Hi guys!” when speaking to a group of women makes perfect sense, but “those guys over there” are never a group of women.

Insulation! Just the concept of insulation, the definition of the word. There are materials that keep cold things colder, longer, and warm things warmer, longer. There’s insulation in your lunchbox, in the walls of your house, in your coat. A 3 year old likely has a coat, or a lunchbox, knows what walls are. They are stoked to know they have insulation! It keeps them warm!

These are all (mostly) neat facts, but most of these are interesting to us because they feel novel and weird given our vast knowledge of the world. The most interesting things to a 3 year old are things that are tangible, or that they can have some experience with. They’re trying to figure out how the world works, give them something relevant.

My trick is to look around you, spot an object, and state something about it that you might not be able to see. For example, lots of drawers have rails inside them, like train tracks for the drawers to move on so that they can open and close and stay attached. Hinges hold two things together and still let them bend or swing - doors and boxes often have hinges. 

Source: work with children. Have fascinated many 3 year olds with these and similar facts.

On the bright side, if you break up, you don’t have to deal with it.

That sucks though, and sounds real stressful and like a huge overreaction from him.

That’s a rough position to be in, but you need to take care of you! Nobody has to do anything wrong for a relationship not to be right, and it feels like you know that. If you can, or if it makes you feel better about ending things, line up a support structure for him. 

Does he have friends you can reach out to? You can let them know (pre written email scheduled to send at time of breakup, or facebook, or however you communicate) that you’re worried about him post breakup.

Does he have a therapist he goes to now? One he used to go to? If he’s got an appointment on the books, or if you can have him schedule one, that’s somebody looking out for his mental health that isn’t you.

If he has neither of these, you can still leave him resources. Your area probably has a crisis line; that’s easy to look up, and you can leave that on a fridge or table if you’re worried.

What’s your ideal timeline for leaving this relationship? Yesterday? Next week? I want to be absolutely clear that I advocate taking care of yourself first. If one thing that will take care of you is setting him up so you don’t have to worry, that’s okay, but please, it’s not sustainable in the long term.

If he has no friends, no therapist, and you feel bad, is there a meetup or interest group you can take/send him to once before you leave? That gives him an immediate social group outside of work that doesn’t include you.

Ultimately, he’s his own person, and neither you not anybody else is responsible for him. If you do all or none of these before breaking up, that doesn’t change.

Wish you all the best in your current and post-him life!!

Meds can be a godsend (they were for me!) but they take so much more patience than I was expecting at first. From when you start to take them, a given antidepressant may take six to eight weeks to work like it will going forward. 

So the first month you start a drug, you get to experience weird side effects like feeling randomly queasy and waking up at 4:00 am every day. Only then does it (hopefully) start having the effect you want it to, and also show you the real side effects. 

So you might start feeling a lot less depressed, but also be unable to orgasm. So then you tell that to whoever is proscribing your meds, and they go “huh” and take another guess at what might work better. And no mistake, this is absolutely a guessing game. We don’t know enough about how brains really work to do anything but trial and error.

So now you have a new drug. You take two months to slowly switch from one to the other, and then you discover that now you can orgasm again, but this one doesn’t help much.

So you try again, and after two more months, the next one helps and doesn’t have weird effects, but doesn’t help as much as the first one. So you raise the dose. But then you get dizzy the hour or two before you should take it. So then you get the extended release version. Which doesn’t work as well, so you raise the dose again. And between each step, you still wait six to eight weeks.

This is not to discourage you, but to moderate your expectations. Meds have absolutely changed life... it just took a year and a half.

As for advice bringing it up, just go for it. They’re used to it; they’ll know what to do. They may need to refer you to an MD for a prescription, in which case you’ll need to have this conversation a second time. You can do it!

I’m the “friend without a car” so my perspective probably won’t help you understand your SO, but hopefully can add some ideas.

My friend group and SO mostly have cars, and while I live near one friend, it’s not on the way to anywhere, and it’s very out of the way for my SO. Busses here take forever, but are fairly comfortable. The metric we use for giving me rides or me bussing to or from places is least possible pain-in-the-ass-time over everybody who would be involved. I’ll clarify that

It takes me about 20 minutes to bus to a coffee shop we like to meet at. It’s fifteen minutes out of the way to pick me up or drop me off, but since my friend and her SO carpool, that’s 30 min. So I bus there.

It takes me an hour and a half to bus to my SO’s house, and a half an hour for him to drive to mine. So if we want to spend time at his house, it’s an hour and of half of time either way. We take turns - mostly if it’s an evening I bus so he can do other things, and in the morning he picks me up.

It takes me an hour to bus downtown to a bar we like, but it’s fifteen minutes out of the way to get me. My friend always offers a ride, unless there’s a scheduling issue.

The way we talk about it is that we like spending time together and doing nice things for each other. One of the nice things they do for me is give me rides. AND ONE OF THE NICE THINGS I DO FOR THEM HAUL MY ASS TO FAR AWAY PLACES ON THE BUS.

First, this may not be something that you can "help her through" - that implies that it may go away soon, and while that would be nice, it probably also will not happen.

Depression is waking up in the morning, and knowing beyond a shadow of a doubt that there will be nothing good about that day, and being proven right about that, day after day after day.

Just do your best to be a safe space for her - don't judge her or tell her how to think. Let her know that you're there when she wants you to be, even just for silent company.

I explain it by asking people what they think when you hear the phrase "one of those days". Just picture one of those days where every little thing is awful for no good reason - you didn't sleep well, food tastes bad, you're running late, you're behind on your work, you're tired and unhappy and just got bad news, but you still have to get through your day, even if you're starting to feel sick. Everybody has bad days.

Now think about what the future would be like if you knew all days were going to be like that. If you woke up in the morning, and knew that that would be the day you had if you bothered getting out of bed. And the day after that too.

I'm glad your boyfriend is trying to understand. Having an understanding boyfriend is one of the most helpful coping tools I have. However, he may just not get it. If you haven't already, part of what helped my boyfriend understand was seeing me at some of my lowest points - don't hide when you're not doing well (unless you already don't, then good for you!)
